objectives: State the role of a DAW.

slides.title: DAWs: the production studio
slides.body:
**DAW (Digital Audio Workstation)**: software that records, edits, mixes, sequences MIDI + audio. The center of modern music production.

**Major DAWs**:
- **Ableton Live**: clip-based + linear hybrid. Strong in electronic + performance. Distinctive Session View.
- **Logic Pro** (Mac-only): Apple. Music creation + light production. Strong included instruments + plugins.
- **Pro Tools**: industry standard for recording + post-production (TV, film). Subscription model.
- **FL Studio** (Windows-first): pattern-based; popular in hip-hop + EDM.
- **Cubase / Nuendo**: Steinberg. Cubase = music; Nuendo = post-production.
- **Studio One**: PreSonus. Modern interface + good for hybrid workflows.
- **Reaper**: lightweight, customizable, cheap (\$60). Power-user favorite.
- **GarageBand**: Apple beginner DAW. Free with macOS / iOS.
- **Bitwig**: modular DAW with extensive routing + the Grid.
- **REASON**: rack-based, modular. Loyal users.

**Common features**:
- **Multi-track recording**: capture multiple inputs simultaneously.
- **MIDI sequencing**: program note data; trigger plugins or hardware.
- **Audio editing**: cut, fade, time-stretch, pitch-shift, crossfade.
- **Plugin hosting**: insert VSTs / AU / AAX into channels.
- **Routing**: complex signal flow between tracks, busses, sends, master.
- **Automation**: time-varying parameter control (volume rides, filter sweeps).
- **Time-stretching + pitch-shifting**: change tempo or pitch without affecting the other (elastic-audio).

**Pricing models**:
- One-time purchase (Logic \$200, FL Studio \$99-499, Studio One \$199).
- Subscription (Pro Tools \$30/mo).
- Free tiers (GarageBand, Reaper for personal use, Cakewalk).

**Workflow philosophies**:
- **Linear timeline**: arrangement on horizontal timeline (Pro Tools, Logic, Cubase). Best for live recording + traditional workflows.
- **Pattern + clip-based**: build patterns + arrange them (FL Studio, Live's Session View). Best for electronic + iterative composition.

slides.title: MIDI: control protocol + ecosystem
slides.body:
**MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface)**: control protocol from 1983. NOT audio. NOT samples. Just messages.

**Message types**:
- **Note On / Off**: 'play note X at velocity Y'. Notes 0-127 (5-octave keyboard).
- **Velocity** (0-127): how hard the note was struck.
- **CC (Control Change)**: parameter control. CC1 = mod wheel, CC7 = volume, CC10 = pan, CC11 = expression. ~120 CCs.
- **Pitch bend**: ±2 semitones (or program-dependent).
- **Program change**: switch patches.
- **Aftertouch**: pressure after note-on.
- **System messages**: clock, sync, sysex (manufacturer-specific data).

**MIDI 1.0**: 7-bit values (0-127). Limited precision; can hear staircase steps in slow filter sweeps.

**MIDI 2.0** (2020): much higher resolution (32-bit). Backwards-compatible. Adopted slowly. New devices ship with MIDI 2.0; many older devices still on 1.0.

**MPE (MIDI Polyphonic Expression)**: standard for per-note expression. Each NOTE has its own pitch + Y-axis + Z-axis CC. Enables expressive per-finger control on devices like ROLI Seaboard, Linnstrument, Lightpad. Modern softsynths (Equator, Arturia Pigments, Native Instruments) increasingly support MPE.

**MIDI → audio chain in a DAW**:
1. Hardware controller (keyboard) sends MIDI to DAW via USB or MIDI cable.
2. DAW records MIDI on a track.
3. Track has a plugin instrument (VST/AU/AAX) loaded.
4. Plugin receives MIDI events, generates audio.
5. Audio routes through track → bus → master → output.

**Tempo sync**: MIDI clock + MTC (MIDI Time Code) sync devices to DAW tempo. Critical for live performance + studio gear integration.

**Velocity layers**: realistic sampled instruments (piano, drums) have different samples per velocity range. 4-16 layers typical for piano; up to 100+ in expensive libraries.

**Articulations + keyswitches**: orchestral libraries trigger different playing styles (legato, staccato, pizzicato, etc.) via 'keyswitches' (MIDI notes outside playing range that switch articulations). Workflow can be cumbersome; some libraries automate via 'expression maps' or DAW articulation tracks (Cubase, Logic 11+).

slides.title: Plugins + the modern ecosystem
slides.body:
**Plugins**: third-party software loaded into DAWs. Massive ecosystem.

**Formats**:
- **VST (Virtual Studio Technology)**: Steinberg. Cross-platform (Win/Mac). De-facto standard.
  - VST2: deprecated (Steinberg ended licensing 2018) but still in use.
  - VST3: current. Newer features (sidechain routing, polyphonic modulation, contextual menus).
- **AU (Audio Unit)**: Apple. macOS / iOS native.
- **AAX**: Avid (Pro Tools). DSP + native variants.
- **CLAP** (CLever Audio Plugin): new open standard. Bitwig + Surge XT-style. Gaining traction.
- **LV2**: Linux open-source.

**Plugin categories**:
- **Instruments (VSTi)**: synthesize sound. Synths, samplers, drum machines.
- **Effects**: process incoming audio. EQ, compression, reverb, delay, distortion, etc.
- **MIDI effects**: process MIDI before instrument. Arpeggiators, chord generators, scale quantizers.

**Notable plugin developers**:
- **Native Instruments**: Komplete suite. Massive (Komplete 14: 100+ instruments + effects).
- **Waves**: classic mixing + mastering. Subscription + perpetual.
- **iZotope**: AI-assisted (RX for repair, Ozone for mastering, Nectar for vocals).
- **FabFilter**: high-quality DSP. Pro-Q (EQ), Pro-L (limiter), Pro-C (compressor).
- **u-he**: high-end synths (Diva, Hive, Repro).
- **Spectrasonics**: Omnisphere, Keyscape — premium sample-based instruments.
- **Universal Audio**: hardware + software emulation (UAD-2 plugins, Apollo interface).
- **Soundtoys**: character processors (Decapitator, EchoBoy).
- **Slate Digital**: mixing console emulation.

**AI-powered plugins** (2022+):
- **iZotope Ozone Master Assistant**: ML-driven mastering suggestions.
- **iZotope RX**: audio repair (de-bleed, de-rumble, voice de-noise) using ML.
- **Adobe Speech Enhance, NVIDIA Broadcast**: real-time AI denoise + enhancement.
- **AI generative tools (Suno, Udio, Riffusion)**: full-song generation. Disrupting + integrating with production workflows.

**Hardware + software hybrids**:
- **Universal Audio Apollo**: DSP-powered interface running UAD plugins with zero latency.
- **Native Instruments Maschine**: groove-box hardware + software integration.
- **Push 3 (Ableton)**: standalone or with Live software.

The plugin ecosystem democratized professional-quality production. A laptop + Logic + a few plugins can produce releases that compete with studios. Genre + style increasingly dictated by accessible tools (vocal chops via Serum, sidechain bass via LFOTool, etc.).

question.question: Build a routing for a vocal track
question.goal: Lead vocal track. Apply: EQ → compression → de-esser. Also send to: parallel-compression bus + reverb bus.

steps.prompt: Insert chain (in order) on the vocal track. Order matters because each processor sees the previous one's output. Suggested order?

options: EQ first (corrective EQ before compression hits), then compressor (controls dynamics), then de-esser (removes sibilance from compressed signal). Some engineers swap compressor/EQ.

steps.reveal: EQ → Compressor → De-esser. Compressor responds to the EQ'd signal; de-esser removes sibilance from compressed (which can EMPHASIZE sibilance).

options: Post-fader: send level rides the vocal fader. As you fade the vocal, parallel compression follows. Most DAW defaults.

steps.reveal: Post-fader: send mix follows vocal level. Pre-fader is for cue mixes (headphone independent of main). For effects sends, post-fader is standard.

options: Post-insert (after all processing): cleaner. The reverb gets a vocal that's already been processed; sounds in context with the dry signal.

steps.reveal: Post-insert: vocal is EQ'd + compressed + de-essed before going to reverb. Reverb sounds more cohesive with dry track. Pre-insert is sometimes desired (different EQ on reverb send) but less common.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Signal chain: EQ → comp → effects, post-fader sends to bus FX}}$$ DAW routing is the practical mixing skill. Sends + busses enable shared effects (one reverb on multiple tracks). Sidechain routing enables side-chain compression. Parallel chains enable subtle layered processing. Mastering this is what separates competent from professional mixing. Modern DAWs (Logic, Pro Tools, Ableton, Studio One) all support these flexibly.

question.question: A DAW is unstable when loaded with many plugins. Likely cause?
options: Plugin instability is common. Suspects: 32-bit plugins on 64-bit DAW, outdated plugins, corrupted preferences, audio buffer set too low (try 512 samples), unstable plugin sandbox. Fix: incremental disabling to find offender + update or sandbox plugin.
question.explanation: Plugin instability remains the #1 DAW pain point. Causes: incompatible plugin versions (legacy 32-bit on modern DAW; old API), DSP errors in poorly-written plugins, audio buffer too low causing dropouts mis-diagnosed as crashes, plugin sandbox (separate process for plugins, isolates crashes). Modern DAWs increasingly sandbox plugins; Logic Pro X+, Ableton 11+ run problematic plugins in isolated processes that can crash without killing the DAW. Workflow tip: bounce hot tracks to audio to free up DSP + plugin load.

slides.workedSolution: Plugin crashes are common. Causes: legacy/outdated plugins, conflicts between plugins, hostile interactions with audio interface drivers, low buffer settings. Sandboxing (Logic, Ableton) isolates plugins in separate processes — a crashed plugin doesn't take down the DAW. Standard practice now. Older DAWs without sandboxing have full-DAW crashes from one bad plugin.

Choosing a DAW for a new producer
question.prompt: A friend asks which DAW to learn. They make pop + electronic, work on Mac, beginner. Walk through the options + recommendation.
Explain in two or three sentences why modern DAWs combine MIDI + audio with deep plugin integration in a single application.
question.rubric: Mentions that music production combines composition (MIDI), recording (audio), processing (plugins), arranging (linear timeline) + mixing — having them in one app eliminates costly format conversions + workflow friction; the plugin ecosystem provides infinite extensibility without changing the core DAW. The all-in-one DAW (vs separate sequencer/mixer/recording tools of pre-90s era) is THE enabler of bedroom-studio production.
